A short tour of the Moon

Seven slides to read aloud, skip around in and paraphrase.

Good evening, and thank you for joining this short tour of the Moon. Over the next few minutes we will look at where it came from, why it changes shape in the sky, and why people still want to go back.
Test: read the narration word for word. The highlight should keep up with you.
Long script

How the Moon was made

  • A young Earth and a planet the size of Mars
  • A giant collision and a ring of molten rock
  • The Moon forms from that ring
Most scientists believe the Moon was born in a catastrophe. About four and a half billion years ago, the young Earth was struck by another world roughly the size of Mars. Astronomers call that lost planet Theia, after a goddess from Greek mythology. The collision was so violent that both bodies partly melted. Enormous amounts of glowing rock were thrown into space, and that debris settled into a hot ring circling the Earth. Gravity then did the patient work. Small clumps pulled in their neighbours, the clumps merged into larger ones, and before long a single large body was orbiting our planet. Some models suggest this happened in only a few thousand years, while others suggest it took much longer. The best evidence came home with the Apollo astronauts. The rocks they collected are remarkably similar to rocks from the mantle of the Earth, but they contain very little water and very few light elements. That is exactly what you would expect from material that was heated and vaporised in a giant impact. So every time you look up at the Moon, you are looking at a piece of the early Earth, flung into orbit by the most dramatic event in the history of our planet.
Test: this script is long enough to scroll. Read on and watch it keep your line a third of the way down. Then skip straight to the last paragraph, "So every time you look up", and check that the paragraphs in between stay unmarked.
Paraphrase

Why it changes shape

  • Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun
  • We see that half from a changing angle
  • The cycle takes about twenty nine and a half days
A common belief is that the phases of the Moon are caused by the shadow of the Earth, but that is not the case. Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun. What changes is how much of that bright half we can see from where we are standing. When the Moon sits between us and the Sun, its dark side faces us and we call it a new moon. Two weeks later it has moved to the far side of its orbit, the whole bright half faces us, and we call it a full moon.
Test: say it in your own words. For example: "Lots of people think Earth's shadow causes the phases, but that's wrong. One half of the Moon is always in sunlight." The highlight should still follow you.
Repeated phrases

Going back

Each reason starts with the same words.

We should go back to the Moon because it teaches us about the early solar system. Its surface has hardly changed in billions of years, so it keeps a record that Earth has long since erased. We should go back to the Moon because it holds frozen water. Ice in the dark craters near the south pole could one day supply drinking water, air and rocket fuel. We should go back to the Moon because it is the nearest place to learn how to live on another world. A rescue is only three days away, which makes it a far safer classroom than Mars.
Test: read the second paragraph, then the third. "We should go back to the Moon because" appears three times, so the highlight should take the next one and not leap to another.
Numbers

The Moon in numbers

384,400 km
Average distance
27.3 days
One orbit
12
People who walked on it
The Moon orbits at an average distance of 384,400 kilometres, and it takes 27.3 days to go around the Earth once. In all of history, only 12 people have ever walked on its surface, and the last of them left in December 1972.

Notes, no narration

Tides

The pull of the Moon raises the oceans twice a day.

This slide has speaker notes but no narration, so the teleprompter follows these notes instead. The gravity of the Moon pulls hardest on the side of the Earth that faces it, and that stretches the oceans into two gentle bulges. As our planet turns beneath those bulges, most coasts see two high tides and two low tides every day.
